lessonTitle: Normal and Tangential Components of Acceleration

blocks.text: A car leaving a motorway on a curved off-ramp feels two different pushes: one along the seat when the driver brakes, and one sideways pressing the passenger against the door. These are the two components of acceleration in path coordinates: one changes the speed, the other changes the direction of travel.

blocks.markdown: **Normal-tangential (path) coordinates** attach a moving frame to the particle. The unit vector $\mathbf e_t$ is tangent to the path in the direction of motion, and $\mathbf e_n$ is perpendicular to it, pointing toward the centre of curvature (the concave side of the path). The velocity is always tangent to the path: $\mathbf v=v\,\mathbf e_t$, where $v$ is the speed in m/s.

blocks.title: Radius of curvature
blocks.text: At each point of a curved path, the path is locally approximated by a circle of radius $\rho$ (m), the **radius of curvature**; its centre is the centre of curvature. On a circular path $\rho$ is the circle's radius, and on a straight line $\rho\to\infty$.

blocks.latex: \mathbf a=a_t\,\mathbf e_t+a_n\,\mathbf e_n,\qquad a_t=\dot v=\frac{dv}{dt},\qquad a_n=\frac{v^2}{\rho},\qquad a=\sqrt{a_t^2+a_n^2}
blocks.caption: The tangential component changes the speed; the normal component changes the direction and always points toward the centre of curvature.

blocks.markdown: The two components do separate jobs. The tangential acceleration $a_t=\dot v$ is positive when speeding up and negative when slowing down. The normal acceleration $a_n=v^2/\rho\ge0$ is non-negative and is zero only on a straight path or when the particle is momentarily at rest. For motion on a circle of radius $R$ at angular speed $\omega$, $v=R\omega$ and $a_n=R\omega^2$, which matches the centripetal term of polar coordinates.

blocks.title: Acceleration of a car on a curve
blocks.prompt: A car moves around a circular bend of radius 80 m at 20 m/s while speeding up at 1.5 m/s$^2$. Find the normal and tangential components of acceleration, the magnitude of the total acceleration, and its angle from the path.

steps.text: Tangential component is the rate of change of speed.
Angle between $\mathbf a$ and the tangent.

blocks.answer: $a_n=5.0$ m/s$^2$, $a_t=1.5$ m/s$^2$, $a\approx5.22$ m/s$^2$, inclined $73.3^\circ$ from the path toward the centre.

blocks.markdown: The same formulas run in reverse to find the **radius of curvature**: if you know the speed and the normal acceleration, $\rho=v^2/a_n$. For a projectile, gravity gives a known acceleration whose component perpendicular to the path is $a_n$. At the apex the velocity is horizontal, so all of $g$ is normal, and $\rho=v_x^2/g$.

blocks.title: Radius of curvature at the apex
blocks.prompt: A ball is launched at 30 m/s at $50^\circ$ above the horizontal (no drag, $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$). Find the radius of curvature of its path at the highest point.

steps.text: At the apex the velocity is horizontal: speed equals the horizontal component.
There the acceleration $g$ is perpendicular to the velocity, so it is entirely normal.

blocks.answer: The radius of curvature at the apex is about 37.9 m.

rows: Path is a known curve (track, road, wire)
Speed and curvature are given; friction and normal reaction align with the axes
Force or acceleration is the same fixed vector (gravity on a projectile)
Constant components, independent integration along each axis
Motion about a fixed centre or rotating arm
Radial and transverse data are the natural measurements
Speed and path curvature both asked
blocks.caption: Selecting a coordinate system.

items: Draw the path and mark the centre of curvature; $\mathbf e_n$ points toward it.
Identify $v$, $\rho$ and $\dot v$ at the instant required.
Compute $a_n=v^2/\rho$ and $a_t=\dot v$; combine as vectors for the total.
Check limits: constant speed gives $a_t=0$; a straight path gives $a_n=0$.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: The normal component is not $\dot v$ and the tangential component is not $v^2/\rho$. Never use the speed of a different instant: $a_n$ changes if $v$ changes, so a car speeding up in a bend has a growing $a_n$. Also remember that $a_n$ always points toward the centre of curvature, never away.

points: Path coordinates split acceleration into $a_t=\dot v$ along the path and $a_n=v^2/\rho$ toward the centre of curvature.
The magnitude is $a=\sqrt{a_t^2+a_n^2}$; on a circle $\rho$ is the radius, and for constant speed $a_t=0$.
Rearranged, $\rho=v^2/a_n$ gives the radius of curvature; choose Cartesian axes for constant force fields and path axes when the path geometry or forces along and across it are given.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a curved path with speed $v$ and radius of curvature $\rho$. The normal component of its acceleration is

options.text: $v^2/\rho$, directed away from the centre of curvature
$v^2/\rho$, directed toward the centre of curvature

questions.correctOptionText: $v^2/\rho$, directed toward the centre of curvature

distractorRationale.a: Magnitude correct but direction wrong: the normal acceleration points inward.

questions.explanation: The normal component produces the change in direction, and it is $v^2/\rho$ toward the centre of curvature. The tangential component $\dot v$ is the separate rate of change of speed.

questions.stem: A car travels around a curve at constant speed. Which statement about its acceleration is correct?

options.text: The normal component is zero but the tangential component is not
Both components are zero because the speed is constant
The tangential component is zero but the normal component is not

questions.correctOptionText: The tangential component is zero but the normal component is not

distractorRationale.c: Constant speed makes only the tangential component zero.

questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector, and the direction of that vector is changing in a curve. With $\dot v=0$ only the normal component $v^2/\rho$ remains.

questions.stem: A particle follows the same circular path of radius 30 m. If its speed doubles from 12 m/s to 24 m/s, its normal acceleration

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $a_n\propto v^2$, so 4.8 m/s$^2$ becomes 19.2 m/s$^2$.
distractorRationale.d: Overcounts: $a_n$ is quadratic, not cubic, in $v$.

questions.explanation: With constant $\rho=30$ m, $a_n=v^2/30$ gives $144/30=4.8$ m/s$^2$ at 12 m/s and $576/30=19.2$ m/s$^2$ at 24 m/s. Doubling the speed quadruples the normal acceleration.

questions.stem: A small bead slides along a fixed circular wire with friction, and you are told the speed and want the normal force and friction. Which coordinate system is most convenient and why?

options.text: Normal-tangential, because the friction and normal force lie along the path axes
Cartesian, because the circle has no preferred direction

questions.correctOptionText: Normal-tangential, because the friction and normal force lie along the path axes

distractorRationale.a: Acceleration is not constant on a circular path.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: forces along and across the path map directly onto $a_t$ and $a_n$.
distractorRationale.c: A circular path is exactly where path axes are simplest.
distractorRationale.d: Gravity is vertical, not radial toward the wire's centre.

questions.explanation: Contact forces are naturally perpendicular and parallel to the path, so path coordinates make each equation of motion involve a single unknown force. Cartesian axes would mix the unknowns through trigonometric terms.

questions.stem: A particle moves at 10 m/s. At an instant, the magnitude of its total acceleration is 8.0 m/s$^2$ and the tangential component is 4.8 m/s$^2$. The radius of curvature of its path is

distractorRationale.b: Not obtained by any consistent route.
distractorRationale.d: Uses the total acceleration as if it were normal: $100/8$.

questions.explanation: The normal component is $\sqrt{a^2-a_t^2}=\sqrt{64-23.04}=6.4$ m/s$^2$. Then $\rho=v^2/a_n=100/6.4=15.6$ m.

questions.stem: A car drives round a circular curve of radius 60 m at a speed of 15 m/s. Find the normal component of its acceleration in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: The normal acceleration is $v^2/\rho=15^2/60=3.75$ m/s$^2$ directed toward the centre. A constant speed means no tangential component.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides on a circular track of radius 18 m. At an instant her speed is 6.0 m/s and increasing at 0.80 m/s$^2$. Find the magnitude of her total acceleration in m/s$^2$.
questions.explanation: Normal component $a_n=36/18=2.0$ m/s$^2$ and tangential component $a_t=0.80$ m/s$^2$. The magnitude is $\sqrt{2.0^2+0.80^2}=2.15$ m/s$^2$.

questions.stem: A stone is thrown from level ground at 20 m/s at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal. Take $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$ and neglect drag. Find the radius of curvature of its path at the instant of launch, in metres.
questions.explanation: At launch, gravity's component perpendicular to the velocity is $a_n=g\cos60^\circ=4.905$ m/s$^2$ (the velocity is $60^\circ$ above the horizontal). Then $\rho=v^2/a_n=400/4.905=81.5$ m.

questions.stem: Explain how you would choose between Cartesian and normal-tangential coordinates for (i) a stone thrown under gravity and (ii) a train travelling along a track of known curvature with brakes applied, and justify each choice.
markingGuide: (i) Gravity is a constant vertical force, so Cartesian components are independent and each is constant-acceleration motion.
(ii) The path geometry is given, and friction or brake forces act along the path while track reaction acts across it, so path coordinates are natural.
Normal-tangential gives $a_n=v^2/\rho$ and $a_t=\dot v$ directly from speed and radius.
Cartesian for the train would need the path equation and its derivatives; path coordinates for the stone mix $g$ into both components that vary along the path.
General principle: choose the coordinates in which the given information and unknown forces appear in simple components.
questions.explanation: A good coordinate system makes the data and unknowns line up with the axes. Constant force fields favour fixed axes, whereas curved guided paths favour axes tied to the path.

questions.stem: Starting from the idea that velocity is always tangent to the path, explain why the acceleration has a normal component even at constant speed, and state the physical meaning of $a_t$ and $a_n$ and the sign of each.
markingGuide: Velocity vector $\mathbf v=v\mathbf e_t$ changes both in magnitude and direction.
Change of magnitude gives $a_t=\dot v$, positive if speeding up, negative if slowing down.
Change of direction of $\mathbf e_t$ gives $a_n=v^2/\rho$ toward the centre of curvature, so it is non-negative.
At constant speed $a_t=0$ but $a_n=v^2/\rho\ne0$ unless the path is straight.
Total acceleration is the vector sum with magnitude $\sqrt{a_t^2+a_n^2}$.
questions.explanation: Acceleration measures change in the whole velocity vector. Magnitude and direction changes are independent, and each gets its own component.
